lead: A sensor often gives a small, noisy voltage riding on a larger unwanted component, such as a DC offset, drift, or 50 Hz mains pickup. Filters decide which frequencies reach the next stage. A pre-amplifier raises the weak signal while adding little noise and presenting a high input impedance. A differential amplifier amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects what both share. An isolation amplifier passes the signal across a barrier, so grounds do not join. Together they turn a raw sensor output into a clean signal for the conditioning chain and for transmission.
prereq: You need signal conditioning for the conditioning chain, and basic op-amp circuits (inverting, non-inverting, virtual short).

blocks.text: A filter is a frequency-dependent voltage divider. It passes a band of frequencies and attenuates the rest. A low-pass filter passes frequencies below its cutoff fc and blocks higher ones. A high-pass filter does the reverse. A band-pass filter passes a band between two cutoffs. A band-stop filter rejects a band. A notch filter is a very narrow band-stop, used to remove 50 Hz mains pickup coupled into long sensor leads.

The cutoff is the frequency where gain falls to 1/√2 = 0.707 of the pass-band value. In decibels that is −3 dB. The order n sets the steepness beyond cutoff: each order adds about 20 dB per decade, or 6 dB per octave, of attenuation. A first-order low-pass has the response below.

blocks.where: H<sub>low</sub> is voltage gain; f is signal frequency in Hz; fc is cutoff frequency in Hz. At f = fc, |H<sub>low</sub>| = 0.707.
H<sub>high</sub> is voltage gain of a first-order high-pass; f and fc are in Hz.

blocks.text: An active filter uses an op-amp to give gain and a low output impedance. The Sallen-Key circuit is a common two-resistor, two-capacitor second-order section. It gives a 40 dB per decade roll-off. Choose the filter before the amplifier when a large out-of-band signal would overload the amplifier. The figure plots the first-order low-pass and high-pass responses against f/fc.

A pre-amplifier is the first amplifier after the sensor. It must add as little noise as possible, because later stages amplify its noise too. At low frequency the pre-amplifier works as a bridging amplifier: input impedance much higher than the source, so a high-impedance sensor such as a piezoelectric element or a thermistor is not loaded. Only when a matched coaxial cable carries a high-frequency signal is the cable terminated in its characteristic impedance (for example 50 Ω) to stop reflections; the amplifier input is then matched to the cable, not to the sensor. Its gain is chosen so the largest expected sensor signal fills the input range of the next stage without clipping.

A differential amplifier has two inputs, V1 and V2, and responds to their difference Vd = V1 − V2. It also responds a little to their average Vcm = (V1 + V2)/2. The differential gain is Ad = Vo/Vd when Vcm = 0. The common-mode gain is Acm = Vo/Vcm when Vd = 0.

blocks.where: Ad is differential gain in V/V; Acm is common-mode gain in V/V; CMRR is in dB. Higher CMRR is better.

blocks.text: A single op-amp difference circuit needs four resistors to set Ad. With 1 % resistors the worst-case ratio for a gain of 100 is about (1 + 100)/(4 × 0.01) ≈ 2500, only 68 dB, whatever the design aimed for. The three op-amp instrumentation amplifier avoids this. Two input buffers give high input impedance and set the gain with one resistor; the third op-amp subtracts the two buffered signals. Laser-trimmed resistor networks give CMRR of 80 dB to 120 dB.

The ECG amplifier puts this section together. The heart gives about 1 mV, the electrodes add up to ±300 mV of DC offset, and the body picks up a 50 Hz common-mode voltage from the mains wiring. The front end is an instrumentation amplifier of modest gain (so the offset cannot saturate it), a high-pass filter near 0.05 Hz to remove the offset, a low-pass at 150 Hz for diagnosis or 40 Hz for monitoring, an optional 50 Hz notch, a driven right-leg electrode that feeds back the inverted common-mode voltage, and an isolation barrier.

An isolation amplifier passes the signal across an insulating barrier. The input side and output side have no direct electrical path. A transformer-coupled isolation amplifier modulates the signal onto a carrier, passes it through a small transformer, and demodulates it. An optocoupler version uses an LED and photodiode or phototransistor; it is compact but slower and less linear. Two ratings matter. The isolation (test) voltage is the short-duration voltage the barrier survives in a factory proof test, usually applied for about one minute. The working voltage is the much lower continuous voltage the barrier can take in service. Choose a part whose working voltage, not just its test voltage, exceeds the highest continuous voltage between the two grounds.

Isolation breaks ground loops. A ground loop forms when two grounded instruments are joined by a signal cable; the small voltage between their ground points drives a current through the cable screen and adds noise. The loop is broken when one instrument floats on the isolated side. In medical equipment, isolation protects the patient from mains fault current through a catheter or electrode: the patient side floats behind the barrier, and the leakage current that can reach a heart-connected electrode is held to about 10 µA in normal use.

Surge protection at the input uses a series resistor or inductor and a clamp, such as a transient voltage suppressor, metal-oxide varistor or gas discharge tube. The clamp limits a lightning surge or switching spike before it reaches the amplifier. Place the clamp after the series resistance so the resistor limits the clamp current. The isolation barrier follows the clamp; it does not replace the clamp.

examples.question: A first-order low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Find its cutoff frequency fc and its gain at 10 kHz in dB. A differential amplifier has Ad = 1000 and Acm = 0.5. Find its CMRR.
steps: Convert R = 1 kΩ = 1000 Ω and C = 0.1 µF = 0.1 × 10⁻⁶ F = 1 × 10⁻⁷ F.
examples.answer: fc = 1591.55 Hz (about 1592 Hz), gain at 10 kHz = 0.1572 (−16.07 dB), and CMRR = 66.02 dB (about 66 dB).
examples.check:
import math
R = 1e3
C = 0.1e-6
fc = 1/(2*math.pi*R*C)
f = 10e3
ratio = f/fc
gain = 1/math.sqrt(1 + ratio**2)
db = 20*math.log10(gain)
Ad = 1000
Acm = 0.5
cmrr = 20*math.log10(Ad/Acm)
print(f'{fc:.2f}')
print(f'{gain:.4f}')
print(f'{db:.2f}')
print(f'{cmrr:.2f}')

examples.question: An ECG amplifier has a differential gain of 1000. The heart gives 1 mV and the body carries 0.5 V of 50 Hz common-mode voltage. (a) Find the output signal and the output hum for CMRR = 100 dB and for CMRR = 60 dB. (b) The offset is removed with a first-order high-pass of R = 3.3 MΩ and C = 1 µF; find its cutoff.
steps: (a) Output signal = A<sub>d</sub> × 1 mV = 1000 × 1 mV = 1.0 V.
At 100 dB: A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub> = 10⁵ (since 20 log₁₀ 10⁵ = 100 dB), so A<sub>cm</sub> = 1000 / 10⁵ = 0.01 and the hum = 0.01 × 0.5 V = 5 mV, 200 times smaller than the signal.
At 60 dB: A<sub>d</sub>/A<sub>cm</sub> = 10³ (20 log₁₀ 10³ = 60 dB), so A<sub>cm</sub> = 1 and the hum = 0.5 V, half the size of the heartbeat; the trace would be unreadable.
Check: 0.048 Hz is below the 0.05 Hz diagnostic limit, so the slow ST segment of the ECG passes while the electrode offset is blocked.
examples.answer: The signal is 1.0 V; the hum is 5 mV at 100 dB CMRR but 0.5 V at 60 dB; the high-pass cuts off at 0.048 Hz.
examples.check:
import math
print(1000 * 1e-3)
print(1000 / 1e5 * 0.5 * 1000)
print(1000 / 1e3 * 0.5)
print(round(1 / (2 * math.pi * 3.3e6 * 1e-6), 3))

traps: Cutoff is the −3 dB point, gain 0.707, not the frequency where gain reaches zero. A first-order filter never reaches zero.
Roll-off is 20 dB per decade per order; a second-order section is 40 dB per decade, not 20.
CMRR calculated from nominal resistor values is ideal. 1 % resistors limit a gain-100 difference circuit to about 68 dB at worst; use a matched network or an instrumentation amplifier.
Isolation voltage is not the same as working voltage; the barrier rating must exceed the fault voltage, including transients.

quiz.q: State the −3 dB cutoff condition of a first-order low-pass filter.
quiz.a: At fc the gain is 1/√2 = 0.707 of the pass-band gain. For an RC low-pass, fc = 1/(2πRC).

quiz.q: Why does a pre-amplifier need high input impedance?
quiz.a: It must not draw current from a high-impedance sensor. Loading the sensor reduces its output and can change its calibration.

quiz.q: A first-order low-pass has R = 2.2 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Find fc.
A differential amplifier has Ad = 500 and Acm = 0.2. Find CMRR in dB.
quiz.a: Ad/Acm = 500/0.2 = 2500. CMRR = 20 log₁₀(2500) = 67.96 dB, about 68 dB.

quiz.q: Why can 1% resistors ruin a designed CMRR?
quiz.a: Common-mode gain depends on resistor ratios. A mismatch converts part of the common-mode input into a differential output. With 1 % parts and a gain of 100 the worst case is about 68 dB, however high the design target.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many signal chains now notch the mains digitally after the ADC, and zero-drift amplifiers cut offset in strain-gauge inputs. Search CMRR trimming and medical isolation standards.
